content: A systematic review and meta-analysis by Fonner and Dalglish evaluated the effectiveness of the dapivirine vaginal ring, though the findings remain unpublished. Palanee-Phillips and colleagues explored the impact of social harms related to male partners on women’s adherence to the ring during a Phase III trial, published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes (JAIDS) in 2018. Their findings emphasized the importance of addressing partner-related challenges to improve adherence. Balkus and colleagues demonstrated in a 2017 study that the use of the dapivirine vaginal ring does not interfere with the effectiveness of hormonal contraception. Another study by Makanani et al. in 2018 examined pregnancy and infant outcomes among women who used the ring during early pregnancy, with results published in JAIDS. Similarly, Kusemererwa and Abasa investigated pregnancy incidence and outcomes in a Phase III trial in Uganda, with findings published in AIDS Research and Human Retroviruses in 2018. The dapivirine vaginal ring has also been evaluated for its potential to influence sexual behavior. Kusemererwa and Abasa conducted a study in 2018 to determine whether the ring led to changes in risky sexual behavior, with results published in AIDS Research and Human Retroviruses. Modeling studies by Glaubius et al. in 2019 assessed the health outcomes, drug resistance, and cost-effectiveness of the ring for HIV prevention, with findings published in the Journal of the International AIDS Society. Another modeling analysis by Smith et al. evaluated the cost-effectiveness of the intravaginal ring, with results accessible through a central database. Reidy and colleagues in 2019 examined the potential impact and cost-effectiveness of the dapivirine vaginal ring as an HIV prevention tool, publishing their findings in PLOS One. Kripke et al. also modeled the potential impact of the ring, with their findings available in a 2021 report. Nel and colleagues conducted a safety and pharmacokinetic trial in 2014 to assess the delivery of dapivirine from the vaginal ring in healthy women, with results published in AIDS. Chen et al. conducted a Phase 2a study in 2019 to evaluate the safety, pharmacokinetics, and acceptability of the ring in postmenopausal women in the U.S., with findings published in Clinical Infectious Diseases. Bunge and colleagues conducted a Phase IIa safety study in 2020 to assess the use of the dapivirine vaginal ring among adolescent women, with results published in JAIDS. Griffin et al. performed a systematic review in 2019 to evaluate the acceptability and preferences for vaginal rings among women in lowand middle-income countries, with findings published in PLOS One. Schwartz et al. explored end-user perspectives on the ability, motivation, and opportunity to use the ring, presenting their findings at the 2020 International AIDS Conference. Ridgeway et al. conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis in 2019 to assess global experiences with vaginal rings, with findings submitted for publication. Nel and colleagues evaluated the safety, acceptability, and adherence to the dapivirine vaginal ring in a multi-country clinical trial in sub-Saharan Africa, with results published in PLOS One in 2016. Van der Straten et al. conducted a Phase I study in the U.S. to assess adherence and acceptability of a multidrug vaginal ring for HIV prevention, with findings published in AIDS Behavior in 2016. Montgomery et al. evaluated the acceptability and use of the dapivirine vaginal ring in a Phase III trial, with findings published in AIDS in 2017. Chitukutaa et al. investigated the impact of negative rumors about the vaginal ring for HIV prevention in sub-Saharan Africa, with findings published in Culture, Health, and Sexuality in 2019. Duby et al. explored reasons why women removed the vaginal ring during menstruation in Malawi, South Africa, Uganda, and Zimbabwe, with findings published in AIDS Behavior in 2020. Laborde et al. examined the impact of the dapivirine vaginal ring on sexual experiences and intimate partnerships in an HIV prevention clinical trial, with findings published in AIDS Behavior in 2018. Nair et al. Van der Straten et al. explored how initial concerns about the ring influenced adherence, with findings published in JAIDS in 2019. Ross and Stover analyzed the relationship between the availability of modern contraceptive methods and their use, with findings published in Global Health: Science and Practice in 2013. Consolidated guidelines on HIV testing services were also reviewed, emphasizing the importance of point-of-care nucleic acid testing for diagnosing HIV in infants and children under 18 months of age. This approach has been shown to significantly reduce the time to diagnosis and treatment initiation, with high-certainty evidence supporting its effectiveness. Studies have demonstrated that same-day point-of-care testing significantly reduces the time to deliver results to caregivers compared to standard laboratory-based testing. This approach also increases the proportion of infants initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART) within 60 days of diagnosis. Cost-effectiveness analyses have shown that point-of-care testing is more cost-effective than standard laboratory-based testing, particularly when integrated with other disease programs such as tuberculosis (TB) testing. Point-of-care testing technologies, such as the Abbott m-PIMA™ and Cepheid GeneXpert®, are already in use for TB and HIV testing in many high-burden countries. These devices are simple to use, require minimal additional equipment, and can perform multiple tests per day. Expanding access to these technologies could significantly improve diagnostic services for HIV and other diseases. Ethical considerations emphasize the importance of equitable access to point-of-care testing for infants, ensuring that they are not disadvantaged compared to other populations. The implementation of point-of-care testing should prioritize high-burden settings and integrate with existing health systems to maximize efficiency and impact. Ongoing research is needed to address quality assurance and sustainable delivery of point-of-care testing for infant diagnosis.
